Putting Out A Fleece
POO-ting out uh flees
slogan (verb phrase)
An idiom drawn from Gideon's sign in Judges 6: laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and asking God to make it wet while the ground stayed dry, then dry while the ground stayed wet, as confirmation of His word. 'Putting out a fleece' has come to mean devising a sign or test and asking God to perform it to confirm guidance — treating Gideon's act as a method to imitate.

Biblical Verdict

🟠
Examine
Gideon's fleece was unbelief graciously accommodated, not a guidance method; God guides by His Word and providence, not by signs we demand.

Biblical Definition

Gideon's fleece (Judg. 6:36-40) was not a model of faith offered for imitation but an instance of weak faith graciously accommodated. God had already given Gideon His clear word — 'Surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man' (Judg. 6:16) — confirmed by an angel, a sign of fire from the rock, and more. The fleece was Gideon asking for still more proof of a promise already plainly given, and even there he confessed his fear of presumption: 'Let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once' (Judg. 6:39). God in mercy stooped to his weakness, but the episode commends God's patience, not Gideon's method. Scripture's settled way of guidance is otherwise: God leads by His revealed Word (Ps. 119:105), by wisdom and counsel (Prov. 11:14), and by His providence ordering circumstances (Prov. 16:9) — not by signs we devise and demand. Indeed the Lord rebukes sign-seeking: 'An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign' (Matt. 12:39), and 'thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God' (Matt. 4:7).

PUTTING OUT A FLEECE, slogan. Devising a sign or test and asking God to perform it to confirm guidance.

Source: Gideon's fleece in Judg. 6:36-40 — wet fleece on dry ground, then dry fleece on wet ground.

Misread as a model: Gideon was asking more proof of a promise God had already plainly given (Judg. 6:16), and feared his own presumption (6:39).

Corrected by Matt. 12:39 ('an evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign') and Matt. 4:7 ('thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God').

Key Scripture

Judges 6:39 — "And Gideon said unto God, Let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once: let me prove, I pray thee, but this once with the fleece; let it now be dry only upon the fleece, and upon all the ground let there be dew."

Judges 6:16 — "And the LORD said unto him, Surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man."

Matthew 12:39 — "But he answered and said unto them, An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas:"

Matthew 4:7 — "Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God."

Psalm 119:105 — "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path."

Proverbs 3:5-6 — "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."

Modern Corruption

Gideon's fleece is misread as a guidance method to copy; it was weak faith graciously accommodated, not a model. God guides by His Word, wisdom, and providence — not by signs we devise and demand (Matt. 12:39; 4:7).

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the error is a misreading of a narrative — turning Gideon's fleece into a technique. The account is told not to give a guidance method but to show God's astonishing patience with a fearful man. The LORD had already spoken with total clarity: 'Surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man' (Judg. 6:16). He had sent an angel, consumed an offering with fire from a rock (6:21), and answered Gideon's first request. The fleece was therefore not faith reaching for guidance but unbelief reaching for one more proof of a promise already given — and Gideon knew it, pleading 'let not thine anger be hot against me' (6:39), conscious that he stood near to tempting God. To read his trembling as a pattern for the believer is to commend the weakness the narrative gently exposes, not the faith it records elsewhere (Heb. 11:32).

The practical danger is that 'putting out a fleece' substitutes a self-devised sign for the means of guidance God has actually appointed. The believer who refuses to act until a parking space opens, a phone rings by a certain hour, or some arbitrary token appears has not exercised faith; he has shifted the weight of decision onto a sign of his own making and called it trusting God. Worse, he edges toward the very thing the Lord forbade in the wilderness: 'thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God' (Matt. 4:7). And he stands under the rebuke of Matthew 12:39 — for it is 'an evil and adulterous generation' that 'seeketh after a sign.' Christian guidance is not the manipulation of providence by tests but trust in the God who orders providence.

The recovery is to seek guidance the way Scripture actually appoints. 'Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path' (Ps. 119:105): the Word is the first and surest guide, settling most questions of duty before any 'leading' is sought. Where the Word does not speak directly, God guides by sanctified wisdom and godly counsel — 'in the multitude of counsellors there is safety' (Prov. 11:14) — and by His providence, for 'a man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps' (Prov. 16:9). The believer trusts in the LORD with all his heart, leans not on his own understanding, acknowledges Him in all his ways, and is content that 'he shall direct thy paths' (Prov. 3:5-6) — without demanding a wet fleece on dry ground to do it.

Hebrew Roots

Gideon's fleece (Judg. 6:36-40) was unbelief graciously accommodated, not a method to copy; God guides by His Word (Ps. 119:105), wisdom, and providence (Prov. 16:9), not by signs we devise — for sign-seeking is rebuked (Matt. 12:39; 4:7).

English: an idiom from Gideon's fleece (Judg. 6:36-40), wrongly taken as a guidance method to imitate.

The narrative's point: Gideon asked more proof of a promise already given (Judg. 6:16) and feared presumption (6:39) — God's patience, not Gideon's method.

God's appointed guidance: Ps. 119:105 (the Word), Prov. 11:14 (counsel), Prov. 16:9 (providence) — not signs demanded; sign-seeking is rebuked (Matt. 12:39).

Usage

"He 'put out a fleece' and waited for a sign, but Gideon's fleece was fear God indulged, not faith God commended."

"Refusing to act until an arbitrary token appears is not trusting God; it edges toward 'thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.'"

"God guides by His Word, by counsel, and by providence — not by wet fleece on dry ground that we demand of Him."
